PRICES CHECKED NOVEMBER 9, 2026 – Deals change quickly, so we will update this page throughout November

Black Friday is a great time to buy AirPods, with retailers competing to offer discounts across Apple’s earbuds and over-ear headphones. Previous sales have brought substantial savings on established models, clearance bargains on older generations, and even discounts on newly released AirPods. But the biggest percentage saving doesn’t necessarily mean the best buy: an older pair needs to be sufficiently cheaper than its replacement to justify missing out on newer features.

Last Black Friday, standard AirPods 4 briefly dropped to $69 in the U.S., while the noise-canceling version fell to $99 – an $80 saving. Even the then-new AirPods Pro 3 received a discount of around $30, while older AirPods Pro 2 reached approximately $139 before selling out. AirPods Max were available for around $400, roughly $150 below their regular price. U.K. savings were more modest, with AirPods 4 at £99 and AirPods Pro 2 at £169, although stock frequently ran out.

This year, we’d watch AirPods Pro 3 and AirPods Max 2 for meaningful discounts, while remaining AirPods 4 and AirPods Pro 2 stock could bring some of the biggest clearance savings. The recently released AirPods 5 may see smaller reductions, making it especially important to compare their price with discounted Pro models. Below, we explain which AirPods to choose and how the offers compare with previous discounts. For savings on Macs, iPads, Apple Watch and more, see our best Apple Black Friday deals.

Which AirPods should you buy this Black Friday?

AirPods Pro 3 – Our best overall choice

Apple

AirPods Pro 3 are especially worth considering if you want strong noise cancellation, a secure in-ear fit, or Apple’s hearing-health features. Their foam-infused ear tips help improve the fit, while an in-ear heart-rate sensor adds another reason to choose them over standard AirPods. Battery life is rated at up to eight hours with noise cancellation enabled.

For most buyers looking for noise-isolating earbuds, these would be our first choice. Older AirPods Pro 2 are worth considering only when the clearance saving is substantial.

U.S. Black Friday price: Amazon has already slashed $50 off the AirPods Pro 3, but we expect the price to go lower. Hopefully by Black Friday they will hit their all-time-low of $169.

U.K. Black Friday price: In the U.K. there’s £19 off the AirPods Pro 3, but we recommend holding out for a better deal.

AirPods 5 – Best for buyers who prefer earbuds without silicone tips

Apple

AirPods 5 offer a lower-cost entry point and an open-ear design for people who don’t like silicone-tipped earbuds. They include Active Noise Cancellation as standard, alongside Transparency mode and Adaptive Audio.

Check which charging case you’re buying. The Wireless Charging Case package adds wireless charging, longer battery life, a Find My speaker, and volume adjustment by swiping the stems. It’s our preferred package when the price difference is small.

U.S. Black Friday price: We’ve not seen a discount yet on the AirPods 5.

U.K. Black Friday price: No savings yet on the AirPods 5.

AirPods Max 2 – Best for over-ear listening

Apple

AirPods Max 2 are the option to consider if you specifically want over-ear headphones. The March 2026 update introduced Apple’s H2 chip and improved noise cancellation, while retaining the premium design and a choice of colors.

We find them difficult to recommend at full price, so the size of the discount matters. Compare any offer with previous sale prices rather than judging it solely against Apple’s asking price.

U.S. Black Friday price: Amazon has the AirPods Max 2 for $449.99, that’s $99 off. They could still go lower though.

U.K. Black Friday price: The AirPods Max 2 aren’t currently discounted on the U.K. Amazon store, but hopefully we will see some good savings towards the end of the month.

Other AirPods – Buy only at a worthwhile clearance price

Apple

AirPods 4 and AirPods Pro 2 can still be worth considering, but compare them with the discounted prices of their replacements. A large reduction from an older model’s launch price can disguise a small saving over a newer, more capable pair.

Check the exact generation, charging case, condition, and seller before buying. For more help choosing, read our AirPods buying guide.

U.S. Black Friday price: We aren’t yet seeing any savings we’d recommend.

U.K. Black Friday price: You can get the AirPods 4 with ANC for £109 at Amazon – that’s only £10 less than AirPods 5, so we’d recommend waiting for that price to go even lower.

Other headphones – Worthy AirPods alternatives

Beats

If AirPods aren’t in your budget, Apple also sells a line of Beats headphones and earbuds that offer many of the same features for a lower price, including the popular over-ear Solo 4 and PowerBeats Pro 2. We’ll also track headphone deals in our round-up of the best earbuds for iPhone and best over-ear headphones if you’d like to see deals on other brands.

U.S. Black Friday price: There is $100 off the Beats Studio Pro and $70 off the Solo 4 at Amazon, but we expect to see more discounts later in November.

U.K. Black Friday price: There is £64 off the PowerBeats Pro 2 and £50 off the PowerBeats Fit at Amazon, but we expect to see more discounts later in November.

Should you buy AirPods now or wait for a better deal?

With Black Friday approaching, we’d avoid paying full price unless you need AirPods immediately. But the sales now stretch across much of November, with some deals already live, so you don’t necessarily need to wait for Black Friday itself. If an early offer is close to a model’s previous low, it can be worth taking: last year’s best deals frequently sold out, and we expect popular offers to go quickly again.

Previous sale prices provide a useful benchmark. We’ve seen AirPods Pro 3 reach $169, while AirPods Max 2 fell to $399 during June Prime Day. An offer above those prices may still be worth considering. Discounts on the Pro 3 can also narrow the gap with standard AirPods, making their extra features more affordable.

For AirPods 5, waiting for a discount makes sense if you aren’t in a hurry: they didn’t receive a significant reduction during October Prime Day. We favor the Wireless Charging Case package when the premium is small. With AirPods Max 2, we’d hold out for a substantial saving rather than pay full price.

Compare retailers as well as generations. Amazon isn’t always cheapest: Walmart and Best Buy also compete on AirPods pricing, while Argos offered competitive U.K. deals last year.

AirPods deals to avoid

When shopping for AirPods, be cautious about older models priced too close to their replacements. Compare the offer with the newer model’s discounted price, rather than judging the saving against an old launch price. Check any conditions attached to offers advertising “free” AirPods, including required spending, contracts, or rebates.

Check the exact version, too. AirPods 4 were sold with and without Active Noise Cancellation, while both AirPods 5 packages include ANC. The Wireless Charging Case version adds features and longer battery life, so a lower price may mean missing out on useful extras. Also check whether the listing is for a new, refurbished, or used pair.

Judge the price against previous offers as well as the advertised discount. A large saving from the recommended retail price doesn’t necessarily mean a particularly good deal if retailers regularly charge less.

Finally, check who is selling and dispatching your order, particularly when shopping through a marketplace. Counterfeit AirPods can be advertised at prices far below those from established retailers. Our guide explains how to tell if AirPods are fake.

How we choose AirPods deals

Macworld’s editors have decades of experience with Apple devices, and our recommendations draw on hands-on AirPods reviews. We consider sound quality, noise cancellation, comfort, battery life, and everyday use – not just the specifications or advertised saving.

Our testing helps us explain which features are worth paying for. For example, our AirPods Pro 3 review assessed how securely the redesigned ear tips stayed in place during exercise, checked battery life against Apple’s claims, and evaluated the heart-rate sensor. Our AirPods Max 2 review weighed their excellent sound and noise cancellation against drawbacks including weight and the Smart Case.

We combine those findings with current prices and previous lows to judge whether an offer represents good value. Our Best AirPods guide explains why the most expensive model isn’t necessarily the best choice for everyone: fit, listening habits, and the features you need all matter.

Along with on-screen awareness and personal context, it’s the final pillar of the advanced capabilities Apple first announced two years ago.

But the latest trend in AI is agents. What started with hobbyist software like OpenClaw has grown into consumer-ready products like Meta’s Muse, OpenAI’s Dots, and Anthropic’s Claude Duet. These AI agents run continuously and somewhat autonomously, taking care of almost anything a person can do online or on their phone or computer. There are some concerns over privacy and safety, and rightfully so, but they have already proven to be very popular.

That is a big step beyond “tell Siri to take actions within apps” and it’s where Ternus would like to take things. Gurman said Apple could make Siri act more like an autonomous agent “as early as next year,” and notes that the company hardly has a choice–announcing such a major feature at WWDC in June would put Apple a year behind the principal players else in the AI space, at least.

Gurman’s report paints the picture of a CEO concerned not just with matching AI companies feature-for-feature, but recognizing the increasing role of AI in computer use in general. Back in October, Apple announced a major security change to macOS. The change involves Full Disk Access (FDA), a permission that, when granted to an app requesting it, allows that app to access protected sections of macOS, such as data caches, mail, backups, and more.

The change is coming in macOS 27.3, which has recently started its developer beta cycle and should be available as a public beta soon. As itspdfu points out in a post, users will need to make the extra effort to allow an app to have FDA. Users will have to go into System Settings > Privacy & Security > Full Disk Access and add the app manually. Previously, the app would be able to add itself to the FDA list and the installer would instruct users to simply toggle on FDA for it.

The reason for the change: AI. “As AI agents become increasingly capable and autonomous, the risks associated with this level of access will grow substantially,” according to Apple in a developer blog post. “We are committed to ensuring users clearly understand these risks before granting such access, so they can make informed decisions about their own data and privacy.”

Itspdfu also states that macOS 27.3 introduces “‘Private Folders,’ a new folder-by-folder permission configured like Full Disk Access.” However, this feature doesn’t seem to be fully capable as of yet.

The macOS 27.3 beta 1 for developers was released on November 2. The official release of macOS 27.3 is expected in December.

How to choose an SSD: Buying advice

You’ve read our recommendations of the best SSDs for Mac owners on the market right now. But how did we reach these decisions, and what general advice should you follow when selecting the best SSD for your needs?

SSDs vs hard drives

Hard drives generally offer more storage for your money, making them a good choice for large backups where capacity matters more than speed. SSDs typically cost more per gigabyte, but provide faster transfers and are usually smaller and lighter. They also have no moving parts, making them better suited to carrying alongside a MacBook.

If you decide in favor of hard drives, see our roundup of the best Mac hard drives.

Which SSD connection should you choose?

For an external SSD, prioritize the connection supported by both the drive and your Mac. A fast SSD can’t deliver its full performance through a slower port or cable. Everyday backups rarely need the fastest connection, while large video projects and frequent transfers can justify paying for USB4 or Thunderbolt.

USB-C doesn’t tell you the speed

USB-C describes the connector’s shape, rather than its transfer speed. Drives with identical-looking USB-C connectors can use different USB or Thunderbolt standards and offer very different performance.

The table below compares connection bandwidth, rather than guaranteed file-transfer speeds.

USB 3.2 Gen 2×2 deserves particular attention. Macs that support USB transfers at only 10Gbps won’t deliver a Gen 2×2 drive’s advertised 20Gbps performance. A Thunderbolt port doesn’t automatically remove that limitation.

To get the most from a Thunderbolt 5 SSD, you need a Thunderbolt 5-equipped Mac. Its higher storage bandwidth can support much faster transfers, but connecting a slower USB drive to that port won’t increase the drive’s own maximum speed.

What about SATA and NVMe?

SATA and NVMe describe the storage technology inside a drive, rather than the external connection to your Mac. SATA SSDs typically top out at around 550MB/s, while NVMe SSDs use PCIe and can achieve substantially higher speeds.

However, an external enclosure’s connection can become the bottleneck. An NVMe SSD capable of several gigabytes per second internally won’t achieve those speeds through a 10Gbps USB connection.

For a ready-made external SSD, our measured performance is more useful than its internal PCIe generation alone. If you’re assembling your own external drive, choose an enclosure that supports your SSD’s type and a connection your Mac can exploit.

Match the drive, port and cable

Use a cable rated for the drive’s connection standard. If you connect through a hub or dock, its supported speeds and shared bandwidth also matter.

Actual transfers depend on file sizes, sustained-write performance and the storage at the other end. Choose a drive based on its tested performance in the kind of work you do, rather than connection bandwidth alone.

How much SSD storage do you need?

Choosing the right external SSD capacity depends on what you plan to store. Capacities vary by model, with several recommendations here extending to 8TB. Allow enough space for your existing files and room for your collection to grow, especially if you work with photos or video.

These starting points can help:

  • 500GB–1TB: Everyday documents, smaller photo collections and transferring files between devices.
  • 1TB–2TB: Larger photo libraries, individual video projects and more substantial everyday storage.
  • 4TB–8TB: Extensive photo and video collections, multiple large projects or substantial backup archives.

For backups, consider how much data you need to protect and allow additional space for older versions you may want to recover. For a working drive, consider the size of your projects and how many you need to keep available at once. A smaller SSD may suffice if you regularly move completed projects to separate storage.

Avoid buying a drive that your files will fill immediately. Leaving free space provides room to grow and can help maintain performance, although the effect of filling a drive varies by model and workload.

Compare the price per terabyte across capacities. Larger models sometimes offer better value, but the highest capacity isn’t automatically the best deal. Balance the price with the space you’ll realistically use.

How portable does your SSD need to be?

Most external SSDs are small enough to carry in a laptop bag, but size, weight and cable design affect convenience. A compact, lightweight drive suits frequent travel, while built-in connectors eliminate a separate cable but may obstruct an adjacent port.

For outdoor use, look for a sturdy enclosure and a stated IP rating for dust and water resistance. Water resistance doesn’t necessarily mean a drive can withstand immersion.

Also consider power requirements. Most portable SSDs draw power from your Mac, but the SanDisk Desk Drive requires mains power, making it better suited to a permanent desk setup.

Shock-proof and rugged?

Other features to look out for include IP-ratings for weather protection and password protection for your important files.

SSDs are more durable than hard drives. They have no moving parts, and are less vulnerable to knocks and movement than mechanical hard drives while writing data. While modern hard drives have some level of shock protection, it’s still a big issue.

However, SSDs can still suffer physical damage or fail, so handle them carefully and keep another copy of important files.

Some portable SSDs even offer water resistance. You can also get ruggedization in a specialized drive enclosure, if you choose to go down the 2.5in drive route.

This is a huge portability benefit. But if they are sat still all day, are SSDs more reliable than HDDs? Hard drives tend to fail mechanically. For example, the motor that spins the platters might burn out. SSDs’ memory cells age, which can lead to failure. Both kinds require specialist recovery. As ever, back up important data.

However, for our purposes, as people who occasionally have to fling drives in rucksacks and plug them in while sat in an airplane seat, SSDs are the clear winner.

How to choose an SSD: Buying advice

You’ve read our recommendations of the best SSDs for Mac owners on the market right now. But how did we reach these decisions, and what general advice should you follow when selecting the best SSD for your needs?

SSDs vs hard drives

Hard drives generally offer more storage for your money, making them a good choice for large backups where capacity matters more than speed. SSDs typically cost more per gigabyte, but provide faster transfers and are usually smaller and lighter. They also have no moving parts, making them better suited to carrying alongside a MacBook.

If you decide in favor of hard drives, see our roundup of the best Mac hard drives.

Which SSD connection should you choose?

For an external SSD, prioritize the connection supported by both the drive and your Mac. A fast SSD can’t deliver its full performance through a slower port or cable. Everyday backups rarely need the fastest connection, while large video projects and frequent transfers can justify paying for USB4 or Thunderbolt.

USB-C doesn’t tell you the speed

USB-C describes the connector’s shape, rather than its transfer speed. Drives with identical-looking USB-C connectors can use different USB or Thunderbolt standards and offer very different performance.

The table below compares connection bandwidth, rather than guaranteed file-transfer speeds.

USB 3.2 Gen 2×2 deserves particular attention. Macs that support USB transfers at only 10Gbps won’t deliver a Gen 2×2 drive’s advertised 20Gbps performance. A Thunderbolt port doesn’t automatically remove that limitation.

To get the most from a Thunderbolt 5 SSD, you need a Thunderbolt 5-equipped Mac. Its higher storage bandwidth can support much faster transfers, but connecting a slower USB drive to that port won’t increase the drive’s own maximum speed.

What about SATA and NVMe?

SATA and NVMe describe the storage technology inside a drive, rather than the external connection to your Mac. SATA SSDs typically top out at around 550MB/s, while NVMe SSDs use PCIe and can achieve substantially higher speeds.

However, an external enclosure’s connection can become the bottleneck. An NVMe SSD capable of several gigabytes per second internally won’t achieve those speeds through a 10Gbps USB connection.

For a ready-made external SSD, our measured performance is more useful than its internal PCIe generation alone. If you’re assembling your own external drive, choose an enclosure that supports your SSD’s type and a connection your Mac can exploit.

Match the drive, port and cable

Use a cable rated for the drive’s connection standard. If you connect through a hub or dock, its supported speeds and shared bandwidth also matter.

Actual transfers depend on file sizes, sustained-write performance and the storage at the other end. Choose a drive based on its tested performance in the kind of work you do, rather than connection bandwidth alone.

How much SSD storage do you need?

Choosing the right external SSD capacity depends on what you plan to store. Capacities vary by model, with several recommendations here extending to 8TB. Allow enough space for your existing files and room for your collection to grow, especially if you work with photos or video.

These starting points can help:

  • 500GB–1TB: Everyday documents, smaller photo collections and transferring files between devices.
  • 1TB–2TB: Larger photo libraries, individual video projects and more substantial everyday storage.
  • 4TB–8TB: Extensive photo and video collections, multiple large projects or substantial backup archives.

For backups, consider how much data you need to protect and allow additional space for older versions you may want to recover. For a working drive, consider the size of your projects and how many you need to keep available at once. A smaller SSD may suffice if you regularly move completed projects to separate storage.

Avoid buying a drive that your files will fill immediately. Leaving free space provides room to grow and can help maintain performance, although the effect of filling a drive varies by model and workload.

Compare the price per terabyte across capacities. Larger models sometimes offer better value, but the highest capacity isn’t automatically the best deal. Balance the price with the space you’ll realistically use.

How portable does your SSD need to be?

Most external SSDs are small enough to carry in a laptop bag, but size, weight and cable design affect convenience. A compact, lightweight drive suits frequent travel, while built-in connectors eliminate a separate cable but may obstruct an adjacent port.

For outdoor use, look for a sturdy enclosure and a stated IP rating for dust and water resistance. Water resistance doesn’t necessarily mean a drive can withstand immersion.

Also consider power requirements. Most portable SSDs draw power from your Mac, but the SanDisk Desk Drive requires mains power, making it better suited to a permanent desk setup.

Shock-proof and rugged?

Other features to look out for include IP-ratings for weather protection and password protection for your important files.

SSDs are more durable than hard drives. They have no moving parts, and are less vulnerable to knocks and movement than mechanical hard drives while writing data. While modern hard drives have some level of shock protection, it’s still a big issue.

However, SSDs can still suffer physical damage or fail, so handle them carefully and keep another copy of important files.

Some portable SSDs even offer water resistance. You can also get ruggedization in a specialized drive enclosure, if you choose to go down the 2.5in drive route.

This is a huge portability benefit. But if they are sat still all day, are SSDs more reliable than HDDs? Hard drives tend to fail mechanically. For example, the motor that spins the platters might burn out. SSDs’ memory cells age, which can lead to failure. Both kinds require specialist recovery. As ever, back up important data.

However, for our purposes, as people who occasionally have to fling drives in rucksacks and plug them in while sat in an airplane seat, SSDs are the clear winner.

Software

Just remember to check that any apps provided by the manufacturer work with Macs as well as Windows PCs.

With the MacBook Pro with PROLED Display, Apple returned the Apple logo to its former glory, switching from shiny aluminum to one that lights up and glows again. And it’s got a new trick: Turn up the display brightness, and the logo gets brighter, too. Turn down the display brightness, and the logo dims.

However, since the brightness controls on the display and logo are linked, the only way to turn the brightness on the logo all the way down is to also turn off the display. And sadly, Apple did not include a system setting control for the logo, so you can’t turn it off by simply flicking a switch.

But you can turn it off through Terminal, Apple’s command line interface for the Mac. In fact, Apple has a support document with the details.

Turn off the glowing Apple logo

  1. You must be logged into the Mac with an account that has Administrator rights.
  2. Launch Terminal. It is in Applications>Utilities. You can also press Command + Space to bring up Spotlight Search, type “Terminal,” and press Return after “Terminal — Open” appears in the search box.
  3. Copy the following and paste it into Terminal sudo defaults write com.apple.CoreBrightness LEBacklightMode -int 0 then press Return
  4. Terminal will ask for your password, which must be a user with Administrator rights. (When typing the password, Terminal will not show the characters.) Press Return and the logo should turn off.
  5. Quit Terminal.

Turn on the glowing Apple logo

Follow the same steps as above, but enter this Terminal command: sudo defaults delete com.apple.CoreBrightness LEBacklightMode

The glowing Apple logo is on by default, so if you reinstall macOS after turning it off, it will turn back on.

Or use can use a new app

Fortunately, now, there’s an app for that. Juan Buis created Backglow, a utility that can be used to customize the glowing Apple logo. In addition to turning it off and on, the free version of Backglow provides settings for two different pulse modes and it can remove the brightness limit. If you pay $9 for Backglow Pro, it activates the ability to set the glow pulse to music, and use Claude Code for your own personal pulse modes.

SanDisk has updated its entire range of portable solid-state drives, including this third-generation update for the Extreme Pro, which, as the name suggests, is aimed at professional users who need high-end performance when working with large video and graphics files.

Sadly, like most forms of memory and storage, the Extreme Pro has rocketed in price since our review of the previous version, now starting at $549.99/£489.99 for a model with 2TB storage, or a whopping $1,099.99/£980.99 with 4TB. The drive did fall a little short on read performance in our tests, using the Blackmagic Disk Speed Test, hitting around 3.5GB/s, but it outperformed on write performance, consistently reaching 4.2GB/s.

Should you buy the SanDisk Extreme Pro?

The SanDisk Extreme Pro combines fast USB4 performance with a slim, lightweight design that’s easy to carry alongside your MacBook. Strong write speeds make it appealing for professionals working with large video and graphics files, while IP65 protection and claimed three-meter drop resistance add reassurance when traveling.

However, read speeds fell short of SanDisk’s claims in our tests, and the lack of Thunderbolt 5 feels disappointing at this price. Starting at $549.99/£489.99 for 2TB, it’s a costly investment. It’s worth considering if portability, durability, and speed are priorities, but the steep price makes it harder to recommend without some reservations.

PROLED MacBook Pro: Display

As the name implies, the tandem OLED display is the key feature of the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display. This is the main reason to spend the extra $400 over the MacBook Pro with a mini-LED backlit display.

When I unpacked the laptop, opened it for the first time, and the display lit up, I instantly knew I was in for a special experience. The brightness of the tandem OLED makes an immediate impression. With the right wallpaper, such as the macOS Golden Gate default photo, the brightness gives the image an aura that feels magical.

It’s an admirable feat to outdo the mini-LED backlit displays that Apple replaced, because they’re excellent displays in their own right. The tandem OLED is more than up to the task. Color saturation and evenness are more pleasing, and the contrast and blacks are deeper. At the Macworld office, my desk is set up with a first-generation Apple Studio Display and a Dell UltraSharp 32 4K QD-OLED Monitor U3226Q, which is made for production work. Yet I prefer looking at the PROLED XDR Display. You will want to work on photos, video, and graphics on this MacBook Pro.

If that work takes you outside, well, don’t worry. I’m currently writing this display section of the review in my backyard, because it’s a perfect San Francisco day, a bright and sunny 68 degrees Fahrenheit (20°C). It’s early afternoon, and the sun is bearing down directly on the display and me. Yet the screen shines through like a champ. Glare and reflections? No problem, thanks to the OLED’s brightness working with the antireflective coating on the glass. Don’t hesitate to go outside or take this MacBook Pro on location. I’d actually stay outside longer if it wasn’t for the fact that the sun is starting to cook me, which makes me a little concerned about the laptop heating up, too.

Roman Loyola/Foundry

Since this is the first time OLED is on the Mac, you might be concerned about burn-in–if you’re going to spend the extra $400, it better last. Only time will tell with the new MacBook Pro, but Apple updated the display engine for OLED, and it monitors the OLED’s condition to maintain optimal performance and minimize the burn-in risk. Apple uses OLED displays in its iPhones, and it introduced a tandem OLED in the iPad Pro in 2024. We haven’t heard of widespread burn-in problems with those devices.

PROLED MacBook Pro: Touch UI

There’s been a lot of anticipation about this being Apple’s first touchscreen Mac. Touchscreen Windows laptops have long been available, and Apple has repeatedly said that touchscreen input on the Mac wasn’t going to happen. Times change. Generations of people have grown up with touch interfaces, and the lack of touch on the Mac is something that prevented some from switching from Windows. There’s a demand for touch.

Roman Loyola/Foundry

I wrote a separate article that details the Touch experience, but here’s the TL;DR version. Apple’s Touch implementation is so good, it can replace the trackpad as your regular input device. Apple didn’t half-ass it here. The company made thoughtful decisions about how the interface should respond to touch, and the result is responsive and reliable. There are a few quirks, but nothing that stops you in your tracks, and you can always retreat to the trackpad.

Touch worked with all the Apple apps and third-party software I tried, but it didn’t work on some games. For example, Resident Evil Village and Total War: Warhammer III do not let you use Touch, and I suspect this is the case for a lot of games that originated on Windows and implement their own maps for input. You probably wouldn’t want to use Touch during gameplay, but it would be convenient when starting a game and navigating its setup screens and settings. Unfortunately, Touch doesn’t work in those situations, either.

Apple

While Apple has done a good job with its first Touch implementation, it’s not a spotlight feature–Touch isn’t even in the name of this new MacBook. I’d go so far as to say that the laptop just happens to have Touch. Apple hasn’t done anything here that requires Touch, so you can buy it, never use Touch, and you won’t miss out on anything. But if Touch is the main reason why you’re considering this laptop, you’ll find it a satisfying implementation, and Apple has gone on record saying it is committed to its development.

PROLED MacBook Pro: Design

Apple took this opportunity to make the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display lighter and a little smaller. Below is a comparison of the dimensions for the 16-inch MacBook Pro models in Apple’s current lineup.

The size difference between the two laptops is inconsequential overall. The feet are slightly recessed as well, so it rests closer to the table and a smidge lower than the standard model, so you’ll get a bit more wiggle room in tight spaces.

Roman Loyola/Foundry

On the other hand, the weight difference is huge. The PROLED XDR Display laptop is 12 percent lighter than the standard MacBook Pro, and that’s noticeable when carrying it around on a bus commute. The laptop’s shell retains the same general design as before, in the same two colors Space Black and Silver. However, the corners of the display are a bit more rounded than before and now the bottom of the display is rounded as well. Also the hinge has been adjusted to better accommodate taps and swipes.

However, since you’ll want people to know you’re using one of these laptops, Apple added a bit of flourish to the back by replacing the shiny aluminum Apple logo with one that glows. It’s a callback to the era when the Mac laptops had the glowing Apple logo from 1999 to 2015. No other MacBook has it, and with its placement on Apple’s most expensive and extravagant laptop, the glowing Apple is now a status symbol.

As with the older implementations, the logo’s brightness is tied to the screen’s brightness. Turn up the screen, and the logo brightens; turn down the screen, and the logo dims. If you want to turn it off completely, you need to use a Terminal command, as detailed in an Apple support document–odd that it’s not an option in System Settings.

PROLED MacBook Pro: Dynamic Island

Did you hate the notch at the top of Apple’s MacBook displays? It’s gone! Rejoice! But it’s not forgotten, because there’s still a camera hole at the top of the display. Apple opted to cut an opening for the FaceTime camera rather than place it under the display as it does with the iPhone Duo‘s inside display. Considering how poor we found the Duo camera’s image quality is, sticking with a cutout (and a smaller one at that) is the right choice. One small side effect: The new camera cutout is slightly lower than the notch was, so it means the menu bar is a little deeper.

Instead of simply replacing the notch with a static pill-shaped cutout, Apple has brought the Dynamic Island to macOS, displaying notifications, Spotlight search, Siri AI, Live Activities, and more. It works as it does on the iPhone. I’m glad it’s on the Mac, but it did take some adjustment, because these elements are now at the top center of the display, whereas before they either popped up in the middle of the display or off to the right.

Roman Loyola/Foundry

An important thing to know is that Live Activities isn’t a feature that’s only for Dynamic Island. In the macOS 27.3 beta, the feature works on other Macs, appearing as a small oval in the menu bar. But it’s much more elegant here.

The FaceTime camera has CenterStage, like the standard MacBook Pro. But it also has advanced video stabilization, which you won’t find on any other MacBook. I’m not sure how crucial this feature is, since I don’t typically move my laptop around while using the camera. But since this laptop is targeted at content creation, it’s a feature Apple felt was necessary.

New laptop, new chip, right? Nope. Apple is using the M5 Pro or M5 Max for the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display, the same chips that were released in the MacBook Pro earlier this year. This decision stems from changes to Apple’s chip development plans in response to growing demand for AI processing. However, the chip series Apple decided to fast-track, the M7, isn’t ready, so M5 chips it is.

The M5 Max is impressive, and fortunately, the major new component of the laptop, the OLED, doesn’t affect chip performance. So, across the board, the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display and the standard model offer the same speed.

If you want the fastest MacBook Pro, it’s the one with the M5 Max chip and the 40-core GPU, tested here. The M5 Max is 26 percent faster than the M4 Max and 45 percent faster than the M3 Max in Geekbench’s Multi-Core CPU benchmark. Geekbench checks the overall CPU performance.

Cinebench is a benchmark tool that uses Maxon’s Redshift render engine, so it’s a good gauge for professionals who handle content. The M5 Max is 18 percent faster than the M4 Max, and 38 percent faster than an M3 Max.

The difference between the M5 Max and M4 Max here isn’t noticeable. They both rely on the built-in encoder on each chip, and Apple didn’t make many changes between the two chips.

A 4K iMovie video export at the High setting was 14 percent faster on the M5 Max than on the M4 Max. With the export set to Best (ProRes), there’s no difference.
